title: Platform Cross-Cutting Scenarios
scopeHtml: Blended production scenarios that combine lifecycle, process death, services, background limits, permissions and manifest policy. Mostly SCENARIO format; each one needs you to pick the right tool from several chunks.

questions.subtopic: Task removal vs process death vs configuration change
questions.promptHtml: A user swipes your app away in Recents. Is that the same as the process being killed, and what survives in each case: rotation, swipe-away, and low-memory kill?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates lump all "state loss" into one bucket. Seniors know three different events with three different survival rules, and pick the right test for each.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Three different events. Rotation recreates the Activity but the process and ViewModel survive. Swipe from Recents removes the task, finishes its activities and, on stock Android, usually kills the process unless something like a foreground service holds it; saved instance state is gone because the task is gone. A low-memory kill takes only the process while the task stays in Recents, so the user comes back to a restored back stack with a fresh process and the saved Bundle. Each needs a different test."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Event               Process   Activity instance   ViewModel   SavedState Bundle   Task in Recents
------------------  --------  ------------------  ----------  ------------------  ---------------
Rotation            same      recreated           survives    delivered           yes
Low-mem kill (bg)   dead      gone                gone        kept by system      yes (restored)
Swipe from Recents  usually   finished            gone        discarded           removed
                    dies*
Force stop (Settings) dead    gone                gone        discarded           removed; also
                                                                                  alarms/jobs cleared
* Stock AOSP: the task is removed, activities finish, and the empty process is killed
  when nothing important is in it. Started services with stopWithTask=true (default)
  are stopped. OEM skins often force-stop more aggressively.
  • Swipe-away is a user intent to leave. The system deliberately does not restore state. Do not try to "resume" after it.
  • Low-memory kill is invisible to the user. The system keeps the task record and each Activity's saved Bundle (held in system_server), and relaunches the process on return. That is the case onSaveInstanceState and SavedStateHandle exist for.
  • Service with android:stopWithTask="false" gets onTaskRemoved(). A foreground service keeps the process at foreground-service importance, so the swipe-away does not kill it.
  • Force stop is stronger than a swipe: the package is put in the stopped state, pending alarms and jobs are removed, and no broadcasts are delivered until the user launches it again.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class SyncService : Service() {
    override fun onBind(i: Intent?): IBinder? = null
    // Manifest: android:stopWithTask="false" so this is called on swipe-away
    override fun onTaskRemoved(rootIntent: Intent?) {
        flushPendingWork()   // short, synchronous cleanup
        stopSelf()
    }
}
adb shell am kill com.example.app          # simulates low-memory kill (only if app is in background)
adb shell am force-stop com.example.app    # simulates Settings > Force stop
adb shell settings put global always_finish_activities 1   # "Don't keep activities"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Testing "process death" by swiping from Recents. That tests a clean start, not restoration.
  • Putting critical persistence in onDestroy, which is not called on kill.
  • Assuming an alarm set earlier still fires after the user force-stops the app. It does not.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does am kill work when the app is in the foreground? → No. It only kills processes that are safe to kill (background/cached), which is why you press Home first.
  2. What does a user see after a low-memory kill? → The task in Recents; on tap the process is recreated, the top Activity is recreated with its saved Bundle, and the rest of the back stack is lazily recreated.
  3. Why did my Service restart after swipe-away? → START_STICKY services are rescheduled by the system after the process dies; verify behaviour on the OEM you care about because some skins force-stop instead.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "state is lost in all three". The senior states which component of state survives each event, which adb command reproduces each, and that swipe-away is intentionally not restored.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team "fixed" a restore bug using swipe-away testing, shipped, and still crashed on 4% of resumes because real low-memory kills left the singleton token null.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping app (300K DAU, mid-range devices) shows a crash cluster in Crashlytics: 1.2% of sessions, almost entirely Android 13/14, only when the app is resumed after >30 min in background. Stack:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Session not initialised
    at com.shop.auth.SessionManager.requireToken(SessionManager.kt:22)
    at com.shop.cart.CartViewModel.refresh(CartViewModel.kt:41)
    at com.shop.cart.CartFragment.onViewCreated(CartFragment.kt:58)

The code:

object SessionManager {
    private var token: String? = null
    fun login(t: String) { token = t }               // called from LoginActivity
    fun requireToken(): String =
        token ?: throw IllegalStateException("Session not initialised")
}
class CartFragment : Fragment(R.layout.fragment_cart) {
    private val vm: CartViewModel by viewModels()
    override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) { vm.refresh() }
}

QA cannot reproduce on emulator; "it works when I rotate". Red herring: crash rate jumped the week a new image-library update shipped.
questions.promptHtml: Find the root cause, reproduce it, and fix it so a user returning after an hour does not crash.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a null check and show a toast", or blames the image library because of the timing. A null check hides the symptom and leaves the user on a broken cart.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does crash correlate with time-in-background (points to process death, not a code regression)? Which screen is the entry point (restored Fragment skipping LoginActivity)? Is the token also persisted anywhere? Any recent targetSdk bump (affects how aggressively I'd expect kills)? Does the crash show up on a cold start (no, only on resume)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix requireToken() to load from persistent storage (EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore) before throwing, and route to login if truly absent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Process death while backgrounded: the system recreates only the top Activity/Fragment; the object is a fresh, empty singleton, and LoginActivity never runs. (b) Image library regression: ruled out by time-in-background correlation. (c) Race between Application init and Fragment: unlikely, since it does not happen on cold start. (d) Multi-process init: would appear on cold start too.
  4. How I'd verify each: Enable Developer options > "Don't keep activities", background the app, return: crash reproduces. Then adb shell am kill com.shop after pressing Home; relaunch from Recents. adb logcat shows Start proc ... for top-activity rather than a normal launch. Check Crashlytics custom key process_start_age_ms (ms since process start): crashes cluster at <2 s after process start.
  5. Root cause: In-memory singleton state is process-scoped. After process death the task record and the Fragment's saved state survive, so the user lands directly on CartFragment in a brand new process whose SessionManager.token is null.
  6. Fix: Short-term: persist token and read lazily.
class SessionManager(private val store: TokenStore) {   // injected, Application-scoped
    @Volatile private var cached: String? = null
    fun token(): String? = cached ?: store.read().also { cached = it }
}
// ViewModel treats null as "needs auth", not as a crash:
if (sessionManager.token() == null) _events.value = Event.GoToLogin else load()

Long-term: state that must outlive the process lives in storage; state needed by a screen goes through SavedStateHandle; the screen has a defined "unauthenticated" state. 7. Prevention: Add "Don't keep activities" to the QA checklist and a UI test that does am kill then resumes; lint/review rule: no object holding mutable user state without a persisted source; Crashlytics key for process age. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not make the token a static cache plus onSaveInstanceState copies in every screen; scattering restore logic invites missed paths. Do not catch the exception globally. Persisting tokens adds a security surface, so use Keystore-backed encryption.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the token expires while backgrounded? → Persisted read returns an expired token; the 401 path must clear it and navigate to login, independent of restoration.
  • Why does rotation not reproduce it? → Rotation keeps the process alive, so the singleton survives.
  • Would a DI-scoped @Singleton be any different? → No, it lives in the process too; only the persistence layer makes it durable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent two sprints chasing a library regression because the crash graph shifted with a release. The correlation was real, but only because the release also moved the process-start time, which changed the kill frequency on low-RAM devices. One adb command reproduced it in a minute.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds a null check or blames the library.
  • Hire: identifies process death, reproduces with Don't-keep-activities, persists the token.
  • Strong hire: also adds process-age telemetry, defines an unauthenticated screen state, and a regression test using am kill.

questions.contextHtml:
A food-order app (80K DAU) shows a "Place order" button. Support tickets: 0.4% of orders are duplicated, charged twice. Backend logs show two POST /orders within 1.5 s from the same session. The button handler:

class CheckoutActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private var inFlight = false
    override fun onCreate(s: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(s)
        binding.pay.setOnClickListener {
            if (inFlight) return@setOnClickListener
            inFlight = true
            lifecycleScope.launch {
                api.placeOrder(cart)           // 2-4 s on slow networks
                inFlight = false
                showSuccess()
            }
        }
    }
}

Tickets mostly mention "I rotated my phone" or "I switched dark mode". Red herring: backend also retries on 5xx via the gateway.
questions.promptHtml: Why do duplicates happen and how do you fix it end to end?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Disable the button on click." That is exactly what the code tries to do; the weak answer misses that the flag and the coroutine both belong to an Activity instance that dies on rotation.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do duplicates have the same idempotency key (none today)? Does the gateway retry POSTs? Is the duplicate request from the same device (yes, same session)? Does the issue appear on devices that rotate or night-mode toggle only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Backend: dedupe by a client-generated order id for a 24 h window. Client hotfix: lock rotation on checkout is a poor idea; skip it.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Rotation/dark-mode recreates the Activity; inFlight is reset to false in the new instance, so the user can tap again; lifecycleScope of the old Activity is cancelled, but the already-sent HTTP request may still complete server-side. (b) Gateway retry. (c) User double-tap race: covered by inFlight.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: tap pay, rotate within 1 s, tap again; watch the server access log. adb shell settings put global always_finish_activities 1 helps too. Compare request ids in the gateway log to separate retries from client duplicates.
  5. Root cause: UI state (inFlight) and work (lifecycleScope) are Activity-scoped. Configuration change destroys both, while the side effect (an HTTP POST) is not cancelled atomically and not idempotent.
  6. Fix:
class CheckoutViewModel(private val repo: OrderRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val orderKey = UUID.randomUUID().toString()   // survive rotation; also put in SavedStateHandle for process death
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<Pay>(Pay.Idle)
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()
    fun pay() {
        if (_state.value is Pay.Loading) return
        _state.value = Pay.Loading
        viewModelScope.launch {
            _state.value = runCatching { repo.place(cart, idempotencyKey = orderKey) }
                .fold({ Pay.Done(it) }, { Pay.Failed(it) })
        }
    }
}

UI observes state and sets button.isEnabled = state !is Loading using the lifecycle-aware collection, so a recreated Activity renders the loading state immediately. Send the key as an Idempotency-Key header. 7. Prevention: Test "action then rotate" in UI tests; code review rule: any non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key; chaos test for retries. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use android:configChanges to dodge recreation: it ignores locale/font/window changes you still must handle, and process death still loses the flag. Don't rely on client-only dedupe; networks retry.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the process dies mid-request? → ViewModel is gone. Persist the key in SavedStateHandle; on return, call a "get order by key" endpoint before allowing retry.
  • Does viewModelScope survive rotation? → Yes, it is cancelled in onCleared, not on recreation.
  • Why not a global inFlight in an object? → Leaks across sessions and dies with the process; it also hides the real bug (non-idempotent endpoint).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments bug looked like a UI problem until we mapped timestamps: the second POST always arrived 0.8-1.4 s after the first, exactly a rotation animation. Adding the idempotency key fixed this and silently fixed two other duplicate sources the team never found.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables button, ignores recreation.
  • Hire: moves state to ViewModel, observes state in UI.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotency key end to end, handles process death for the key, and rejects configChanges as a fix.

questions.contextHtml:
A messaging app (1.1M DAU) shows a "Mark as read" action on notifications. Analytics: 3% of "mark as read" actions processed twice, and "Reply" sends the previous message's text on some devices. Code:

val intent = Intent(ctx, NotificationActionReceiver::class.java)
    .setAction("com.chat.MARK_READ")
    .putExtra("conversationId", convo.id)
val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(
    ctx, 0, intent, PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
builder.addAction(R.drawable.ic_check, "Mark read", pi)

Server logs show action requests arriving 40-300 ms apart. Targets API 34. Red herring: users on a flaky network.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both bugs and design the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a debounce in the receiver." That hides the duplicate but not the wrong-conversation issue, which is the real tell.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Multiple conversations notified at once? Do different conversations get different notification ids? Is the receiver doing network work directly? Are duplicate rows on the server with identical ids?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make the server endpoint idempotent on (conversationId, lastMessageId); ship a client fix soon.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) PendingIntent identity: two PendingIntents are the same if Intent.filterEquals matches (action, data, type, class, categories; extras are ignored) and the requestCode matches. All conversations share requestCode 0 and action, so FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT makes the second conversation's extras overwrite the first's. (b) Double delivery: user taps twice quickly on a heads-up notification that stays visible until the receiver cancels it. (c) Receiver doing async work after returning, so process is killed and the broadcast re-delivered: unlikely.
  4. How I'd verify each: Post two notifications from a debug build, tap the first action: the logged conversationId is the second's (confirms identity collision). adb shell dumpsys notification --noredact shows the PendingIntent per notification; adb shell dumpsys activity broadcasts while tapping twice. Check the receiver's logs for two invocations with the same notification_id.
  5. Root cause: Extras do not take part in PendingIntent identity; a constant requestCode shares one PendingIntent across notifications. Duplicates come from no in-flight guard and a notification that is not removed synchronously.
  6. Fix:
val requestCode = convo.id.hashCode()               // or a unique stable int per conversation
val intent = Intent(ctx, NotificationActionReceiver::class.java)
    .setAction("com.chat.MARK_READ")
    .setData(Uri.parse("chat://convo/${convo.id}"))  // data makes filterEquals unique too
    .putExtra("conversationId", convo.id)
val pi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, requestCode, intent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
// Receiver: cancel notification first, then enqueue idempotent work
class NotificationActionReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) {
        val id = i.getStringExtra("conversationId") ?: return
        NotificationManagerCompat.from(c).cancel(id.hashCode())
        markReadWork.enqueueUnique(id)               // WorkManager unique work, KEEP policy
    }
}
  1. Prevention: A unit/instrumented test that posts two notifications and asserts the extras per PendingIntent; code review rule: requestCode or data must be derived from the entity id.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: hashCode() can collide; for large id spaces use a data URI instead. Don't use FLAG_MUTABLE to "fix" it (security risk, and unnecessary). Don't do the network call inside onReceive without goAsync() or WorkManager.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENT? → It invalidates the previous PendingIntent, which breaks a still-visible older notification action.
  • What about Reply with RemoteInput? → The PendingIntent for RemoteInput must be FLAG_MUTABLE on API 31+ because the system fills in the result; scope it to an explicit intent.
  • Does the receiver need to be exported? → No, explicit intent to your own class; keep exported=false.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A chat app replied to the wrong person for months. The fix was a one-line requestCode change, but the audit afterwards found three more places using constant requestCodes with UPDATE_CURRENT.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: debounce only.
  • Hire: explains filterEquals/requestCode and fixes identity.
  • Strong hire: adds idempotent server and receiver work, correct mutability for RemoteInput, and a test.

questions.contextHtml:
The security team flags your app after a pentest. Findings: a manifest receiver PaymentResultReceiver has an intent filter and no exported attribute; a dynamically registered receiver DownloadDoneReceiver accepts broadcasts from any app; a service SyncService is exported with no permission. You also plan to bump targetSdk 33 -> 34 next sprint. QA's smoke run on an Android 14 build after the bump produced:

java.lang.SecurityException: com.shop: One of RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED should be specified when a receiver isn't being registered exclusively for system broadcasts
    at android.app.ContextImpl.registerReceiverInternal

Red herring: the crash only occurs on Android 14 devices.
questions.promptHtml: Plan the audit and the bump without breaking partners who legitimately send you broadcasts.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set exported=false everywhere." That breaks the payment partner app that really does send you results, with no migration plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which external apps legitimately call us (partners, same-publisher apps)? Do they hold a signature or just a package name? Do we own the sender code? What is our minSdk (affects ContextCompat.registerReceiver)? Any analytics SDK registering its own receivers via manifest merge?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship the fixes behind a normal release; nothing is exploited yet, but disable unnecessary exported components at once.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what the audit will find): (a) Android 12+ (targetSdk 31): components with intent filters must declare android:exported explicitly or install fails; some already "work" because current targetSdk predates it. (b) Context-registered receivers: Android 14 (targetSdk 34) requires RECEIVER_EXPORTED or RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED unless only system broadcasts. (c) Library receivers/providers merged into the manifest with wrong flags. (d) Internal broadcasts that should be explicit, setPackage, or a Flow/SharedFlow instead of a broadcast.
  4. How I'd verify each: ./gradlew :app:processReleaseManifest and read build/intermediates/merged_manifests (or Android Studio "Merged Manifest" tab) to find every component with exported="true"; aapt2 dump xmltree on the APK; adb shell dumpsys package com.shop | grep -A3 Receiver; test sending from adb shell am broadcast -a ... -n and from a sample third-party app to confirm what is reachable. Lint: ExportedReceiver, UnprotectedSMSBroadcastReceiver.
  5. Root cause: Defaults are historical: pre-31 components with filters were exported by default. Nobody had an inventory of who needs what.
  6. Fix:
<!-- internal only -->
<receiver android:name=".DownloadDoneReceiver" android:exported="false"/>
<!-- partner needs it: lock down with signature permission or sender check -->
<permission android:name="com.shop.permission.PAYMENT_RESULT"
    android:protectionLevel="signature"/>
<receiver android:name=".PaymentResultReceiver"
    android:exported="true"
    android:permission="com.shop.permission.PAYMENT_RESULT">
    <intent-filter><action android:name="com.shop.PAYMENT_RESULT"/></intent-filter>
</receiver>
ContextCompat.registerReceiver(
    this, downloadDone, IntentFilter("com.shop.DOWNLOAD_DONE"),
    ContextCompat.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED)       // handles API < 33 for you

Signature permission only works if the partner is signed with your key; otherwise use an allowlist (verify caller via a PendingIntent/getSentFromUid on API 34+ where available, or an authenticated payload such as an HMAC token). Never trust extras alone. 7. Prevention: CI step that fails if the merged manifest contains new exported="true" entries without a reviewed allowlist; lint set to error. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't blanket-flip to false before checking partner traffic (breaks integrations silently). Don't mark things RECEIVER_EXPORTED just to silence the crash.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Is a local broadcast better? → LocalBroadcastManager is deprecated; use an in-process Flow or explicit broadcasts.
  • Do system broadcasts need the flag? → Not if the filter only contains protected system actions.
  • A library adds an exported activity; how do you fix it? → tools:node="remove" or override with exported="false" in your manifest.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A fintech discovered an exported receiver that triggered a refund-status refresh on any broadcast. Harmless on its own, but it was reachable from any installed app and a precursor to a real intent-redirection chain found a month later.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: flips everything to false.
  • Hire: audits the merged manifest and handles the API 34 registerReceiver rule.
  • Strong hire: signature permission/allowlist for real partners, CI guard, and a plan for library components.

questions.contextHtml:
A photo-scanner app (200K DAU) crashes for ~0.8% of users in the camera screen with:

java.lang.SecurityException: Permission Denial: opening provider ... or
java.lang.RuntimeException: Fail to connect to camera service
    at android.hardware.Camera.<init>

Support: "I turned off camera in Settings, switched back, app crashed / lost my work". Some reports say the app restarted with a blank screen. Red herring: the crash also shows on devices whose camera is in use by another app.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you make the app robust to permission changes while it is running or backgrounded?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Check permission once at startup." The permission can be revoked at any time after startup.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the camera screen restored after process death directly (skipping the permission flow)? Does the app save in-progress scans? Which API level? Do the crashes occur on Android 11+ where auto-reset applies?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap the camera open in a permission check and handle SecurityException by returning to the permission screen.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) User revokes CAMERA in Settings while the app is backgrounded; Android kills the process; on return the system restores the camera screen in a new process without re-running the permission request. (b) Auto-reset of unused app permissions (Android 11+, targetSdk 30+) after months of non-use. (c) Camera busy by another app (the red herring). (d) Permission granted only "while using the app"/one-time (Android 11+), which expires when the app leaves foreground.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell pm revoke com.scan android.permission.CAMERA while the app is open: the process is killed. adb shell dumpsys package com.scan | grep -i camera for the granted state. adb logcat | grep -i "Killing.*permission"; ActivityManager logs "Killing ... (adj ...): permissions revoked". Test one-time grant with the system dialog.
  5. Root cause: Runtime permissions are revocable at any time and the check happened once per process, not per use. Revocation kills the process, so restored UI can reach the privileged call before any permission UI.
  6. Fix:
override fun onStart() {
    super.onStart()
    if (ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
        == PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) startCamera()
    else permissionLauncher.launch(Manifest.permission.CAMERA)   // registerForActivityResult
}

Check at the point of use (onStart / before opening), handle denial with a rationale and a "Open Settings" path when shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale is false after a prior denial. Also persist the scan draft, so a kill does not lose work. 7. Prevention: Test matrix: grant, deny, deny-twice, one-time, revoke while foreground, revoke while background, auto-reset. Instrumented test using UiAutomation.revokeRuntimePermission. Crashlytics key for permission state. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't cache "isGranted" in a field or singleton. Don't request on app start, but at the moment of need. Don't loop the system dialog.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why can't I re-prompt after two denials? → From Android 11, a second denial is treated as "don't ask again"; the request returns denied immediately, so send the user to Settings.
  • What changes on one-time permission? → Granted until the app is in the background for a while (the system revokes after the process goes away or after a timeout); always re-check in onStart.
  • Where does restoration put the user? → On the same screen; every privileged screen needs its own gate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A scanner team had a flawless permission flow on a fresh install but a bug cluster from users who revoked camera for privacy during a trip and came back. The gate was in the onboarding Activity only.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: startup-only check.
  • Hire: check at point of use, handle revoke -> process death.
  • Strong hire: covers one-time, auto-reset, Settings deep link, draft persistence, and automated revoke tests.

questions.promptHtml: Your crash dashboard shows issues that QA cannot reproduce. Give me a repeatable matrix of platform conditions to try before declaring "cannot reproduce".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many "unreproducible" bugs are one of a small set of platform events. The signal is whether you have a systematic checklist and the adb knowledge to trigger each.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I run the app under six forced conditions: process death, activity recreation, configuration changes, background restrictions, permission changes, and low memory. Each has a one-liner: Don't keep activities, am kill, wm density/size, locale and dark mode switches, cmd appops/pm revoke, and am send-trim-memory. If the crash correlates with time in background or with a specific OS version, I pick the condition from that signal."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Symptom clue                        Condition to force                      Command
---------------------------------   --------------------------------------  --------------------------------------------
Crash on resume after long idle     Process death                           adb shell am kill <pkg>   (after Home)
Crash on any screen revisit         Activity destroyed in bg                adb shell settings put global always_finish_activities 1
Crash after rotate/dark/locale      Config change                           adb shell cmd uimode night yes; wm size/density
Crash after language change         Locale                                  Settings > per-app language
Missing data after hours            Doze / standby                          adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle
                                                                            adb shell am set-standby-bucket <pkg> rare
Crash after Settings toggle         Permission revoked                      adb shell pm revoke <pkg> <perm>
OOM/slow on low devices             Memory pressure                         adb shell am send-trim-memory <pkg> RUNNING_CRITICAL
Crash only with OEM                 Aggressive kill                         Test on that device; adb shell am force-stop
  • Start from Crashlytics keys: OS version, device RAM class, process age, foreground/background state at crash, time since last foreground.
  • Pair with adb logcat -b crash and adb shell dumpsys activity processes.
  • Compare the stack top: NullPointerException in a ViewModel/singleton right after a Fragment's onViewCreated is the classic process-death signature; IllegalStateException: Fragment not attached suggests lifecycle race; ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException means background-start limit.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Custom keys make unreproducible bugs reproducible
FirebaseCrashlytics.getInstance().apply {
    setCustomKey("process_age_ms", SystemClock.elapsedRealtime() - Process.getStartElapsedRealtime())
    setCustomKey("is_foreground", ProcessLifecycleOwner.get().lifecycle.currentState.isAtLeast(Lifecycle.State.STARTED))
}

(Process.getStartElapsedRealtime() is API 24+.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using only emulators with plenty of RAM; kills happen on 2-3 GB devices.
  • Testing process death by swiping from Recents (different event).
  • Forgetting to restore settings (always_finish_activities 0, cmd uimode night auto).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you tell process death from a crash in the logs? → Absence of an exception; am_proc_died / "Process ... has died" in the events log; relaunch shows Start proc ... for top-activity.
  2. How do you test Doze? → dumpsys deviceidle force-idle after unplugging (dumpsys battery unplug), then step back with dumpsys deviceidle unforce.
  3. How do you automate this in CI? → Instrumentation tests using ActivityScenario.recreate() and UiDevice to press Home then am kill; run on a Firebase Test Lab low-RAM device.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Try rotating." Senior: a table of forced conditions, driven by telemetry clues, with automation for the top three.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cluster that "appeared only on Tuesdays" was actually users who left the app overnight on low-RAM devices, where process death after hours in the background is common.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (2M DAU) sends push notifications with an https://news.example/article/123 deep link. Users report: tapping the notification while the app is open opens a second ArticleActivity on top; Back then walks through duplicate screens; from a cold start, Back exits to the launcher instead of the home feed. Manifest:

<activity android:name=".ArticleActivity" android:exported="true"
    android:taskAffinity="com.news.article" android:launchMode="singleTask">
    <intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW"/>
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT"/>
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE"/>
        <data android:scheme="https" android:host="news.example" android:pathPrefix="/article"/>
    </intent-filter>
</activity>

Notification PendingIntent is getActivity(ctx, 0, Intent(ACTION_VIEW, uri), IMMUTABLE). Recents shows two cards for the app since a recent release added the taskAffinity. Red herring: the link verification is passing.
questions.promptHtml: Explain what the task system is doing and propose the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use singleTask and CLEAR_TOP everywhere." That is already half-applied and is the cause of the second Recents card.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed in the last release (the taskAffinity addition)? Which Activity hosts the home feed and is it the LAUNCHER? Is onNewIntent handled? Does the same deep link come from the browser and from our notification?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the custom taskAffinity (revert to default package affinity) in a hotfix; it is the reason for the separate task.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Custom taskAffinity plus singleTask places ArticleActivity in its own task: a second Recents card, and Back from it leaves the app. (b) onNewIntent not overridden, so the existing instance ignores the new article id and the user sees stale content (looks like "duplicate"). (c) Notification intent lacks a synthetic back stack: starting an Activity directly has no parent. (d) Browser-originated links use NEW_TASK from another app, behaving differently from notification taps.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -E "Task|ArticleActivity|affinity" to view tasks and affinities; adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d https://news.example/article/123 from cold and warm; check Recents. Log intent.flags in onCreate and onNewIntent.
  5. Root cause: Task placement is decided by launchMode, taskAffinity and intent flags together. A different affinity moved the Activity into a separate task; with no TaskStackBuilder parent chain, Back has nowhere sensible to go.
  6. Fix:
<activity android:name=".ArticleActivity" android:exported="true"
    android:launchMode="singleTop"
    android:parentActivityName=".HomeActivity">
// Notification: build a proper synthetic back stack
val pi = TaskStackBuilder.create(ctx)
    .addNextIntentWithParentStack(
        Intent(Intent.ACTION_VIEW, uri, ctx, ArticleActivity::class.java))
    .getPendingIntent(articleId.hashCode(),
        PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
// ArticleActivity
override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent); setIntent(intent); viewModel.load(intent.data)
}

singleTop reuses the instance only if it is at the top; TaskStackBuilder ensures Home sits underneath. 7. Prevention: A test matrix of {cold, warm, article-open, other-activity-open} x {notification, browser, adb}; a rule requiring review for taskAffinity/singleInstance changes. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: singleTask clears everything above the instance, which can destroy a reading flow; reserve it for true entry points. Don't use FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP blindly on deep links, it drops user context.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What does singleTask do with a different affinity? → Looks for an existing task with that affinity, else creates one.
  • Why setIntent in onNewIntent? → getIntent() otherwise returns the original launch intent, so later reads (e.g. after recreation) are stale.
  • Does autoVerify affect task behaviour? → No, it only affects whether the link opens the app without a chooser.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-mode tweak made to fix one duplicate screen created a second Recents card and a Back-exits-app bug. The reviewer had assumed "affinity" was a harmless label.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: random flags.
  • Hire: identifies affinity and onNewIntent issues, uses TaskStackBuilder.
  • Strong hire: full test matrix, explains tradeoffs of singleTask vs singleTop and verifies via dumpsys.

questions.contextHtml:
A music app (900K DAU) bumps targetSdk 33 -> 34. Within a day, Crashlytics shows a new cluster on Android 14 only: 6% of playback starts crash.

android.app.MissingForegroundServiceTypeException: Starting FGS without a type  callerApp=ProcessRecord{... com.music} targetSDK=34
    at android.app.ActivityThread.handleCreateService

After a partial fix adding foregroundServiceType="mediaPlayback" to the manifest, a second stack appears for 1.5%:

java.lang.SecurityException: Starting FGS with type mediaPlayback ... requires permissions: all of the permissions allOf=true [android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK]

Also, with the screen off for 20-30 minutes on some Android 12+ devices, playback stops and logs show ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException when it tries to restart.
questions.promptHtml: Walk through every issue and the correct service design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add the type in the manifest." That fixes one of three problems and misses the permission and background-start rules.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are we on Media3 MediaSessionService or a hand-rolled Service? Where is startForeground called (and with which overload)? Who starts the service: UI, notification action, Bluetooth media button, or a restart job? Does stack 3 come from background?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: declare both the type and the matching permission; keep a staged rollout at 5% to confirm the crash rate falls.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) For targetSdk 34, every FGS must declare at least one type in the manifest and pass a matching type to startForeground; omission throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException. (b) Each type also needs its own normal permission (FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK), plus the base FOREGROUND_SERVICE. (c) Starting an FGS from the background is restricted since Android 12 (API 31); apps cannot restart playback from a background job. (d) Service killed under pressure and restarted via START_STICKY from background: not an allowed context.
  4. How I'd verify each: Read the merged manifest; run on Android 14 emulator at targetSdk 34 and trigger each start path. adb shell dumpsys activity services com.music shows isForeground=true and foregroundServiceType=0x2. For (c) reproduce with adb shell am start-foreground-service from a shell while the app is not visible, and use adb shell cmd deviceidle force-idle.
  5. Root cause: Three separate platform rules (typed FGS in 14, per-type permission in 14, background start limit in 12) were all hit by one bump. The restart path assumed the old "service can start itself anytime" model.
  6. Fix:
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK"/>
<service android:name=".PlaybackService" android:exported="true"
    android:foregroundServiceType="mediaPlayback">
    <intent-filter><action android:name="androidx.media3.session.MediaSessionService"/></intent-filter>
</service>
ServiceCompat.startForeground(this, NOTIF_ID, notification,
    ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_MEDIA_PLAYBACK)

Use Media3 MediaSessionService, so the framework manages foreground/notification transitions; media button events and MediaController connections are exempt paths to start playback. Wrap risky background starts in try/catch (ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException) and degrade to a user-visible notification instead of crashing. 7. Prevention: targetSdk bump checklist from the behaviour-changes page; instrumented test per start path; staged rollout with a crash-rate gate. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't pick a loose type like specialUse to dodge review; Play policy declarations apply. Don't hold wakelocks to compensate for kills.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user pauses and the service is not foreground? → The process drops to cached importance and may be killed; on resume you restart from a user-visible context (activity, notification action, media button).
  • Can a notification action restart it? → Yes, a user tap on a notification action is an allowed exemption from background-start restrictions.
  • Verify on developer.android.com: the exact list of exemptions evolves.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The team shipped the type fix and the permission fix in two hotfixes, 36 hours apart; testing only on one emulator image hid the permission error.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: manifest type only.
  • Hire: type + permission + background start handling.
  • Strong hire: Media3 design, exemptions, rollout gate and test per start path.

questions.contextHtml:
A ride-sharing driver app (150K drivers) starts a location FGS when a trip request arrives via FCM data message. After a targetSdk 33 -> 34 bump and a backend change that sent the request as normal priority data messages, ~9% of requests fail:

android.app.ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: startForegroundService() not allowed due to mAllowStartForeground false: service com.ride/.TripService
    at android.app.ContextImpl.startServiceCommon

Drivers say the app "didn't wake up". Phones are mostly Android 12-14, mostly on battery, 40% Xiaomi/Samsung. Red herring: the crash does not show in debug builds, which are exempt because the dev keeps the app in the foreground.
questions.promptHtml: Why does the start fail, and how do you make dispatch reliable?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WorkManager instead." That ignores the user-visible driver flow and the real exemption rule.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: FCM priority on these messages? Are we using notification messages or data? What is the "request to accept" SLA (10 s?)? Do drivers have an "online" shift state we can use to keep a visible FGS running?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Backend: set priority: high and ttl short on trip requests; client: catch the exception and fall back to a high-importance notification with a full-screen intent.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Normal-priority FCM does not grant the background FGS start exemption; high-priority FCM does (and it can start a service for a limited window). (b) Under Doze/standby, normal priority is deferred, so by the time we run we are not in an allowed state. (c) OEM battery manager restricts the receiver. (d) Using a Worker to launch the FGS, which isn't exempt.
  4. How I'd verify each: FCM diagnostics dashboard: delivery priority vs "restricted priority" (getPriority() vs getOriginalPriority() on RemoteMessage) and log them. adb shell dumpsys deviceidle force-idle then send a test message. adb shell dumpsys activity service com.ride | grep -i fgs. Compare buckets: adb shell am get-standby-bucket com.ride.
  5. Root cause: Android 12+ forbids starting FGS from the background except in exempt cases; the backend change dropped a high-priority message to normal priority, removing the exemption, and the client has no fallback.
  6. Fix:
override fun onMessageReceived(m: RemoteMessage) {
    try {
        ContextCompat.startForegroundService(this, Intent(this, TripService::class.java).putExtra("id", m.data["id"]))
    } catch (e: ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException) {   // API 31+
        notifier.showTripRequest(m.data["id"]!!)               // heads-up + tap to open
        Telemetry.log("fgs_denied", m.priority, m.originalPriority)
    }
}

Keep drivers' "online" mode as a persistent, user-visible FGS (location type with FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION and location permission) so no background start is needed. Server: trip requests always high priority, and only for user-visible, time-sensitive events (abuse leads to FCM de-prioritisation). 7. Prevention: Alert on getOriginalPriority != getPriority; contract test that backend sets priority high; load test in Doze. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't set all messages to high priority; FCM may downgrade. Don't poll with exact alarms every 10 s (battery, policy). Don't ask users to disable battery optimisation as the primary strategy.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the driver has "restricted" standby bucket? → High-priority FCM still delivers but quotas apply; the always-on "online" FGS avoids relying on it.
  • Can the app use a full-screen intent? → Only for calls/alarms category; on Android 14 a USE_FULL_SCREEN_INTENT is granted by default for those apps only; verify on developer.android.com for eligibility.
  • Does an FGS started from FCM need a type? → Yes, on targetSdk 34 with a permission and a matching manifest type.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A backend refactor changed a single enum default from HIGH to NORMAL. Client crash rate climbed only on battery-saving phones, and the root cause lived in a service nobody on mobile owned.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swap to WorkManager.
  • Hire: knows high-priority FCM exemption and adds fallback.
  • Strong hire: telemetry on priority downgrade, persistent online FGS, server-client contract.

questions.contextHtml:
Play Console reports 5.1% user-perceived ANR rate (bad-behaviour threshold is 0.47% overall in Play vitals; verify the current value on Android vitals docs), concentrated in Samsung and Xiaomi mid-range devices with 3 GB RAM. Typical trace of the main thread:

"main" prio=5 tid=1 Native
  at android.os.BinderProxy.transactNative(Native Method)
  at android.os.BinderProxy.transact(BinderProxy.java:xxx)
  at android.content.pm.IPackageManager$Stub$Proxy.getInstalledPackages(...)
  at android.app.ApplicationPackageManager.getInstalledPackages
  at com.app.analytics.DeviceInfo.collect(DeviceInfo.kt:44)
  at com.app.MainActivity.onCreate(MainActivity.kt:71)

Other clusters show ContentResolver.query and Settings.Secure.getString on main. Input dispatch timeout logs: Input dispatching timed out ... Waiting to send non-key event because the touched window has not finished processing. Red herring: a recent Compose upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: How do you diagnose and eliminate main-thread binder ANRs at scale?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Move it to a coroutine." True but incomplete: no method to find all of them, no budget and no guard against regressions.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of ANRs have BinderProxy.transact at top of main? Are they on cold start or steady-state? Does system_server load correlate (other apps starving the binder pool)? Which SDKs are calling?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move DeviceInfo.collect off main and make it lazy; remote-disable the analytics collection via a config flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Our own synchronous getInstalledPackages/getPackageInfo calls in onCreate: with several hundred packages the reply is large (and may need multiple pages), slowed by a busy system_server. (b) Third-party SDKs doing binder calls in ContentProvider.onCreate/App Startup. (c) Provider queries to slow processes (the callee is cold-starting). (d) Settings/TelephonyManager calls blocking when the remote service is stalled. (e) Compose: red herring, no trace evidence.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group ANR stacks by the first non-framework frame in Play Console; capture a Perfetto trace with binder_driver, sched, am categories and look at the main thread's "binder transaction" slices; StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(...detectAll().penaltyLog()) in debug and on a beta cohort; adb shell dumpsys binder_calls_stats and /d/binder/transaction_log (debug builds of the OS). adb pull /data/anr on a repro device.
  5. Root cause: A binder call is a synchronous IPC to another process; its latency is the callee's latency plus the queue to a free binder thread, not ours. On loaded low-RAM devices that tail exceeds seconds, and main-thread callers inherit it.
  6. Fix:
class DeviceInfoRepo(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val pm: PackageManager) {
    val packages: Deferred<List<String>> = scope.async(Dispatchers.IO, start = CoroutineStart.LAZY) {
        pm.getInstalledPackages(0).map { it.packageName }
    }
}
// Application: StrictMode in debug
StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(StrictMode.ThreadPolicy.Builder().detectAll().penaltyLog().build())

Also: query only the needed package (getPackageInfo(name)), cache results, add <queries> correctly, and use App Startup with deferred initializers. 7. Prevention: Gate on a main-thread budget in CI (Macrobenchmark startup + jank); a Detekt/lint rule banning PackageManager, ContentResolver and Settings calls in onCreate; StrictMode in internal builds that crashes on violations (penaltyDeath). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't wrap in runBlocking on IO "just to be safe" (it blocks main again). Don't use GlobalScope. Lazy loading moves latency to first use: guard UI that needs it with a loading state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why are some ANRs not caused by our code at all? → The main thread can be blocked by CPU starvation or a stalled system_server; the trace shows Native + BinderProxy; check CPU stats in the ANR file (CPU usage from ...).
  • How does the platform decide input ANR? → 5 s input dispatch timeout; broadcasts 10 s foreground / 60 s background; services 20 s foreground / 200 s background (verify per version).
  • Does coroutine IO guarantee safety? → The IO dispatcher has 64 threads by default; blocking binder calls there are fine but unbounded fan-out can starve it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 4.6% ANR rate dropped under 0.4% after we moved six SDK initialisations out of onCreate. The surprise was that two of them were ours, in a "utility" called from the splash screen.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "use coroutines".
  • Hire: reads ANR traces, finds binder callers, moves off main.
  • Strong hire: StrictMode/Perfetto method, SDK audit, CI budget, understands callee latency.

questions.contextHtml:
You bump targetSdk 34 -> 35 for a 1.5M DAU banking app. QA on Android 15 reports: toolbar overlaps the status bar, bottom navigation hides behind the gesture bar, dialogs cut off, and the login button is covered by the keyboard. Also, a crash at launch on a few devices:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Only fullscreen opaque activities can request orientation

(on Android 8.0 only; unrelated to the bump). Release is in 10 days; Play requires targeting 35 by the deadline. Red herring: the layout looks fine on Android 14 after the bump.
questions.promptHtml: What changed, how do you ship safely, and what is your risk plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Set the opt-out attribute." The opt-out is temporary, and was removed for apps targeting 36.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What share of users is on Android 15 today (the behaviour is enforced by OS version when targeting 35, i.e. only Android 15+ devices see it)? Views or Compose? Any custom windows (dialogs, bottom sheets, popups)? Any other 35 changes (16 KB page size readiness, FGS timeouts, predictive back)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not applicable to production yet; choose between delaying the bump (check the Play policy deadline and extension option) and the temporary opt-out android:windowOptOutEdgeToEdgeEnforcement (style item in a values-v35 theme) as a bridge.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Edge-to-edge is enforced for apps targeting 35 on Android 15: windows draw behind system bars; fitsSystemWindows-less layouts overlap. (b) Dialogs/bottom sheets inherit enforced edge-to-edge too. (c) adjustResize behaviour with ime insets changes if the app handled the keyboard manually. (d) Hard-coded status bar colour calls no longer have effect (status/navigation bar colours are transparent by enforcement).
  4. How I'd verify each: Android 15 emulator, run all key flows; adb shell am compat enable/disable for the change id (EDGE_TO_EDGE_ENFORCED, find via adb shell am compat list); layout inspector; screenshot tests with inset simulation; Espresso with InsetsController.
  5. Root cause: The platform now assumes apps handle WindowInsets; legacy layouts assumed the system reserved space.
  6. Fix:
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        enableEdgeToEdge()                       // androidx.activity 1.8.0+: backports to older APIs
        super.onCreate(b)
        ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(binding.root) { v, insets ->
            val bars = insets.getInsets(WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars() or WindowInsetsCompat.Type.displayCutout())
            val ime = insets.getInsets(WindowInsetsCompat.Type.ime())
            v.updatePadding(bars.left, bars.top, bars.right, maxOf(bars.bottom, ime.bottom))
            WindowInsetsCompat.CONSUMED
        }
    }
}

Compose: Scaffold with innerPadding, Modifier.imePadding(), safeDrawingPadding(). Adopt edge-to-edge for all API levels in the same release (call enableEdgeToEdge on every Activity), so behaviour is consistent and testable on Android 14 too. Keep the opt-out only as a fallback behind a flag in values-v35. 7. Prevention: Screenshot tests for each screen with gesture/3-button nav and cutouts; a staged rollout (1% -> 5% -> 20% -> 100%) monitored for layout complaints and crash rate; document the policy before the next bump (36). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't ship the opt-out as the long-term plan: the attribute stops working at targetSdk 36 (verify). Don't bump without testing with 3-button nav; most overlap bugs appear there.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Android 14 look fine? → Enforcement is OS 15 + targetSdk 35; Android 14 follows the old behaviour.
  • What else in 35 might bite? → Typed FGS timeouts (dataSync), 16 KB page size for native libs on new devices, BOOT_COMPLETED FGS limits, and predictive back changes.
  • How do you ship with limited time? → Land enableEdgeToEdge() earlier in a release that still targets 34, then bump targetSdk later.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: We bumped and shipped a day before the Play deadline; the first hotfix was for a keyboard-covered login on 3-button navigation, caught by nobody because every tester used gestures.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: opt-out only.
  • Hire: handles insets and IME, tests on Android 15.
  • Strong hire: decouples edge-to-edge from the bump, staged rollout, screenshot tests, awareness of the next deadline.

questions.contextHtml:
A video-calling app declares a :call process for the call service. After adding Firebase Analytics init and a local database migration to Application.onCreate, support reports: "chat history empty after a call" and "app uses lots of battery". Logs:

I/App: Application.onCreate pid=14211 process=com.vc
I/App: Application.onCreate pid=14388 process=com.vc:call
I/Db: running migration 41 -> 42   (twice, 3 ms apart)
E/SQLiteDatabaseLockedException: database is locked

Code:

class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        Analytics.init(this)
        Database.migrate(this)       // opens and migrates app.db
        TokenStore.refreshAsync()
    }
}
<service android:name=".CallService" android:process=":call" android:exported="false"/>
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a lock around migrate." Locks are per-process; the two processes do not share memory.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why is the call service in its own process (isolation from main crashes)? What state does it need (tokens, db)? Does the database use WAL mode? Is Application subclass shared by all processes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Guard heavy init by process name in a hotfix; the :call process should not run the migration.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Every process of the app instantiates the Application class and calls onCreate, so init runs twice, each with its own static state. (b) Two processes run the migration concurrently, so database lock and partial migration. (c) Duplicate analytics and token refresh double the battery cost. (d) In-memory singletons (cache, token) are not shared across processes, so the call process reads stale data.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log Application.getProcessName() (API 28+) or ActivityManager.runningAppProcesses in onCreate; adb shell ps -A | grep com.vc shows two pids; Perfetto or logcat counts of init logs per pid; adb shell dumpsys activity processes.
  5. Root cause: Process = separate VM + separate statics. Application.onCreate is per process, so global initialisation must be process-aware, and cross-process shared state must go through IPC or a store with proper multi-process semantics.
  6. Fix:
class App : Application() {
    override fun onCreate() {
        super.onCreate()
        val isMain = Application.getProcessName() == packageName       // API 28+
        if (isMain) {
            Analytics.init(this)
            Database.migrate(this)
            TokenStore.refreshAsync()
        } else {
            CallProcess.init(this)         // minimal: logging, crash reporting
        }
    }
}

For API < 28, match your pid against ActivityManager.getRunningAppProcesses() to find your process name. The :call process reads data through the main process via a bound service/ContentProvider, or uses a database opened in WAL mode with enableWriteAheadLogging(); do migrations only in the main process, and make the call process wait on a "db ready" signal. 7. Prevention: A startup-time test that counts init invocations per process; review rule for any new android:process; document the process map. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use SharedPreferences for cross-process sync (not process-safe). Don't use MODE_MULTI_PROCESS (deprecated, unreliable). Don't mix ContentProviders with initialization order assumptions (providers also init per process).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which init runs first in a new process? → ContentProvider onCreate runs before Application.onCreate, so Startup initializers run per process.
  • Why have a separate process at all? → Memory isolation (crash or OOM does not take the UI), heap limit per process, ability to restart independently; costs: IPC, double init, memory baseline.
  • Does android:process change the Application class? → No, same class, one instance per process.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tidy-looking :push process doubled cold-start CPU because it initialised the whole DI graph. The fix cut 18% of battery attribution in vitals.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: lock.
  • Hire: process-aware init.
  • Strong hire: cross-process data design, WAL, ContentProvider init order, justification for the process.

questions.contextHtml: A medication-reminder app (400K DAU) hears from support: "Reminders do not ring on my Xiaomi/OnePlus/Samsung phone." 11% of tickets. Telemetry: of scheduled reminders, 94% fire on Pixel, 62% on Xiaomi. The app uses setExactAndAllowWhileIdle for reminders and a foreground-less background JobScheduler job to resync. Product asks: "Make it work on every phone, no matter what the vendor does." Red herring: the notification channel importance is correct.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do, and what do you tell product?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Tell users to disable battery optimisation" as the whole answer, or "add a foreground service forever".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are reminders life-critical (medical)? Can we measure per-OEM fire rate and delay? Is the app force-stopped or just killed? Do alarms disappear after reboot or after a "clean" in the vendor task manager? Do we have USE_EXACT_ALARM justification (Play policy for alarm/clock apps)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: In-app health check: detect missing alarm (compare expected vs observed) and show a banner to the user to fix settings; add a reliable server-side fallback (high-priority FCM at reminder time with a notification).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Vendor skin kills or force-stops background apps after swipe or screen-off, deleting alarms (force-stop clears alarms on AOSP too). (b) Aggressive battery policies restrict autostart so BOOT_COMPLETED is not delivered to re-arm. (c) Exact alarm permission denied (Android 14 default for new installs targeting 33+) so fallback to inexact. (d) Doze deferral on setExact not AllowWhileIdle.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare scheduled vs delivered timestamps per Build.MANUFACTURER; adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep com.med to check the alarm is registered; adb shell dumpsys deviceidle; after swipe-away vs force-stop. Check AlarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms() result in telemetry; PowerManager.isIgnoringBatteryOptimizations. Use dontkillmyapp-style knowledge to see vendor settings, but verify on real devices.
  5. Root cause: Vendors add proprietary kill policies outside AOSP guarantees; an app that relies on in-process scheduling (no server fallback, no health check) has no recourse.
  6. Fix: Layered design:
    • Exact alarm with a permission check and declared reason: if (!am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) startActivity(Intent(Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, Uri.parse("package:$packageName"))). Use USE_EXACT_ALARM only if the app's core function qualifies (alarm clock, calendar) and policy allows.
    • Re-arm on BOOT_COMPLETED, MY_PACKAGE_REPLACED, TIME_SET, TIMEZONE_CHANGED.
    • Server-driven backup: high-priority FCM at reminder time.
    • A guided onboarding to exempt battery optimisation (ACTION_REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS has a Play policy restriction; check), with an honest explanation per OEM.
    • Delivery telemetry and in-app "missed reminder" recovery.
  7. Prevention: Per-OEM canary dashboards; a device lab with Xiaomi, OnePlus, Samsung; contract that "reminders are best effort" in product copy.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't promise 100% delivery. Don't run a permanent FGS just to survive vendor policy: policy violation and battery cost. Don't add hacks for specific OEMs' hidden intents without a fallback (they break across ROM versions).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does Pixel work? → AOSP semantics: exact alarms persist across swipe-away and Doze; only force-stop clears them.
  • Is a 3 AM reminder with a screen-off phone different? → Doze applies; setExactAndAllowWhileIdle is rate-limited (about once per 9 minutes per app in Doze; verify).
  • When is an FGS appropriate? → User-initiated, ongoing work (a timer in progress), not as a persistence hack.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Delivery on one vendor jumped from 62% to 88% only after a server-side FCM fallback; the in-app settings guide added another 4 points but was brittle after ROM updates.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "ask users to whitelist".
  • Hire: layered reliability with re-arming and telemetry.
  • Strong hire: managed expectations with product, server fallback, permission flows, policy awareness.

questions.contextHtml: A video-sharing app (3M DAU) uploads 200 MB-1.5 GB videos. Today an UploadService (started service) runs the upload. Complaints: 14% of uploads fail when the user leaves the app; logs show Process ... killed by system (cached) and, on Android 12+, ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException when the retry job restarts it. PM wants "uploads that never fail, with a notification progress bar, and no scary battery warnings". Median upload takes 4 min on Wi-Fi, 25 min on 4G. Red herring: backend p95 latency of 400 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Choose the architecture. WorkManager, foreground service, or both? Justify with platform constraints.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use WorkManager, it is the recommended API." Without addressing long-running work, user-initiated expectations, constraints, and resumability, this is a slogan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the upload user-initiated and visible? Must it survive reboot? Is the server resumable (chunked/tus)? Do we need to run on metered networks? What is the maximum acceptable delay for background completion?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop restarting a started service from the background; surface "upload paused" with a tap-to-resume notification.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) A plain background service is killed once the app leaves foreground (background limits since API 26, process to cached). (b) Starting FGS from background is blocked (API 31+). (c) Non-resumable upload means every kill restarts at 0%. (d) Network handoff (Wi-Fi to cellular) breaks the connection.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys activity services com.vid; adb shell am kill; Perfetto for process state transitions; server logs for chunk offsets; test on airplane-mode toggles; check WorkInfo.stopReason (API 31+ getStopReason, WorkManager 2.9+) after stops.
  5. Root cause: Long-running user-visible work was modelled as a service with no guaranteed execution contract, and the upload had no resumability.
  6. Fix: Use both, layered:
    • WorkManager as the durable scheduler: OneTimeWorkRequest with NetworkType.CONNECTED, backoff, unique work per upload id, state in Room.
    • Inside the worker, call setForeground(ForegroundInfo(...)) (CoroutineWorker) with a notification and the right FGS type, so the work gets foreground priority while visible. Since the work is user-initiated and may exceed normal windows, on Android 14+ evaluate setExpedited (quota-limited) vs user-initiated data transfer jobs (API 34 JobInfo.Builder.setUserInitiated(true) with RUN_USER_INITIATED_JOBS permission; WorkManager support is limited, verify the library version).
    • Resumable protocol: chunk size 5-8 MB, persisted offset; retry resumes at the last acknowledged chunk.
class UploadWorker(ctx: Context, p: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(ctx, p) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result {
        setForeground(createForegroundInfo(0))          // type dataSync; see Q386 for timeout
        return try { uploader.resume(inputData.getString("id")!!) { pct -> setForeground(createForegroundInfo(pct)) }; Result.success() }
        catch (e: IOException) { Result.retry() }
    }
}
  1. Prevention: Telemetry for each stop reason; chaos tests (kill, network flip); upload success rate SLO by device class.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Pure FGS gives immediacy but no persistence across reboots/kills; pure WorkManager gives persistence but not instant start or long window without foreground info. Don't hold a permanent wakelock. Don't hide behind "dataSync" without handling its Android 15 timeout.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Where does an alarm fit? → Not for uploads; alarms trigger work, not perform it.
  • What if the user force-stops? → WorkManager work is cancelled; it resumes only when the user next opens the app.
  • Do we need a notification permission on Android 13+? → Posting the notification needs POST_NOTIFICATIONS, but the FGS notification still shows in the task manager if denied; plan UX for the denial.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team replaced a custom service with plain WorkManager and the failure rate dropped, but time-to-start for user-visible uploads rose; the fix was setForeground for visible jobs and a quiet background class for auto-backups.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one API, no reasoning.
  • Hire: WorkManager + foreground info + constraints.
  • Strong hire: resumability, user-initiated jobs, quotas, timeouts, telemetry.

questions.contextHtml:
A habit-tracker app (500K DAU) targets API 34 and schedules reminders:

alarmManager.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, triggerAt, pi)

Crash cluster on fresh installs on Android 14 (2.3% of new users):

java.lang.SecurityException: Caller com.habit needs to hold android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM or android.permission.USE_EXACT_ALARM to set exact alarms.

Existing users upgrading from older versions are fine. The manifest declares SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM. Red herring: users who disabled notifications.
questions.promptHtml: Why does a declared permission still fail, and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Request it at runtime with the permission launcher." It is not a runtime-dialog permission.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the app really a clock/calendar (eligibility for USE_EXACT_ALARM)? Does a +/- 10 minute window hurt users? Fresh vs update installs? Android version spread?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Wrap in canScheduleExactAlarms(); fall back to inexact setAndAllowWhileIdle.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Android 14: SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is no longer pre-granted for newly installed apps targeting 33+; it is a special permission the user grants in Settings (it is auto-granted only when upgrading from a state where it already was). (b) Backup/restore edge cases. (c) User revoked in Settings (app killed, alarms cleared). (d) Missing declaration: ruled out.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell appops get com.habit SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM; adb shell cmd appops set com.habit SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM deny then retest; adb shell dumpsys alarm | grep -A3 com.habit; telemetry canScheduleExactAlarms() on fresh installs.
  5. Root cause: Exact alarms became a gated, user-controlled capability to protect battery; the code assumed a manifest declaration was enough.
  6. Fix:
fun schedule(at: Long, pi: PendingIntent) {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < 31 || am.canScheduleExactAlarms()) {
        am.setExactAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, pi)
    } else {
        am.setAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, at, pi)      // window of imprecision
        promptUserOnceForExactAccess()                                 // Settings.ACTION_REQUEST_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM
    }
}
// Re-schedule when the user grants access:
// <receiver> action AlarmManager.ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED

Don't use USE_EXACT_ALARM unless the app's core function is alarm clock/calendar (Play policy). Habit reminders rarely need to-the-second precision. 7. Prevention: Test on fresh-install Android 14 images; detect permission revocation, re-arm alarms after ACTION_SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM_PERMISSION_STATE_CHANGED. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't spam the user to enable exact alarms. Don't use a foreground service as an alarm replacement. Exact alarms cost battery; many "reminders" are fine with inexact windows.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What happens when the permission is revoked? → The app is killed and its exact alarms are cancelled; re-schedule on next launch or on the state-changed broadcast.
  • How are setAlarmClock alarms different? → They show a system alarm icon and are exempt from some restrictions, but are intended for alarm-clock UX.
  • What about Doze and setExact (no AllowWhileIdle)? → Deferred until a maintenance window.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team treated the SecurityException as a rare device bug; a month later the dashboard showed it was every fresh install on API 34.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tries runtime request.
  • Hire: canScheduleExactAlarms + fallback.
  • Strong hire: policy-aware USE_EXACT_ALARM decision, re-arm on state change, product trade-off.

questions.contextHtml:
After a redesign, a chat app (700K DAU) crashes on 0.9% of backgrounding events:

java.lang.RuntimeException: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException: data parcel size 1048392 bytes
    at android.app.servertransaction.TransactionExecutor...
    at android.app.ActivityThread$H.handleMessage
Caused by: android.os.TransactionTooLargeException
    at android.os.BinderProxy.transactNative

Code in the conversation screen:

override fun onSaveInstanceState(out: Bundle) {
    super.onSaveInstanceState(out)
    out.putParcelableArrayList("messages", ArrayList(adapter.items))   // up to 2,000 messages, ~700 B each
    out.putParcelable("draftPhoto", draftBitmap)
}

Red herring: the crash does not occur on tablets.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the numbers, fix it, and prevent recurrence.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compress the bitmap." It treats the symptom and ignores the 1 MB shared buffer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Android versions (14 made the throw more visible via targetSdk behaviour in some paths)? Does it occur on stop (state save) or on startActivity with large extras? How large are the largest conversations?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the list and bitmap from the Bundle in a hotfix; load from DB on restore.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Bundle > ~1 MB: 2,000 x 700 B = 1.4 MB, plus a bitmap. (b) Per-process transaction buffer shared across concurrent transactions, so the effective limit is under 1 MB. (c) Fragment saved state adds to the Activity's. (d) Large result from a content query: not here.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log Bundle size with Parcel.obtain().apply { writeBundle(b) }.dataSize(); the AndroidX Bundle size debugging; adb logcat | grep -i "Transaction"; run with adb shell dumpsys activity to see saved state; test with a 2,000-message conversation in debug.
  5. Root cause: onSaveInstanceState data goes via Binder to system_server (so the state survives process death). The Binder transaction buffer is about 1 MB (1 MB minus overhead) shared by all in-flight transactions of the process.
  6. Fix:
class ChatViewModel(private val state: SavedStateHandle, private val repo: ChatRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val conversationId: String = state["id"]!!            // tiny: only keys
    val messages = repo.observeMessages(conversationId)    // Room is the source of truth
}
// draftPhoto: save to cache file; keep only its Uri string in SavedStateHandle

Rule of thumb: keep saved state well under ~50-100 KB; store IDs, scroll position, and short text. Use Room/DataStore/files for the rest. 7. Prevention: A debug-only StrictMode-like check measuring Bundle size on save, logging above 100 KB; UI test with large data; code review rule banning collections in Bundles. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't catch the exception: the system loses your state silently. Don't stash big data in static singletons (dies with the process). Persisting adds I/O; do it off main.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does it happen on stop for target 24+? → State is saved in onStop on API 28+ (after onStop), earlier before it; so large saves can block or fail in the background.
  • Where else do you see it? → startActivity extras, setResult data, notifications' PendingIntent extras, AIDL parameters.
  • What is a safe size? → No guaranteed number; keep it tiny. 1 MB is a shared budget, not yours alone.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The crash only appeared in the field because test data had 20 messages. After the fix we added a BundleSizeGuard that reported p99 saved-state size to analytics; it found two other screens at 300 KB.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: compress.
  • Hire: explains 1 MB buffer and moves data to DB.
  • Strong hire: measures, SavedStateHandle usage, guardrails, and knows the other entry points.

questions.contextHtml:
A fitness-tracker app (600K DAU) restarts its step-tracking foreground service after reboot. After raising targetSdk to 35, 4% of Android 15 users report that tracking does not resume after a phone restart; Crashlytics has:

android.app.ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException: Starting FGS with type health callerApp=... targetSDK=35 ... BOOT_COMPLETED

(or, for an app of the mediaPlayback variety, the same error for type mediaPlayback). Receiver:

class BootReceiver : BroadcastReceiver() {
    override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) {
        if (i.action == Intent.ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED)
            ContextCompat.startForegroundService(c, Intent(c, StepService::class.java))
    }
}

Manifest type is health. Red herring: the receiver is declared and fires (logcat shows onReceive).
questions.promptHtml: Why does it fail on 15 only, what is allowed, and how do you design boot-time tracking?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Request battery optimisation exemption." That does not change the FGS-from-boot rule.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which FGS type? (Android 15 blocks BOOT_COMPLETED receivers from launching certain types: dataSync, camera, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, mediaProjection, microphone; verify the current list.) Does health appear in that list for our type? Do we need continuous tracking or can we use the sensors batch API?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Catch the exception; on boot, schedule a WorkManager job or show a "tap to resume tracking" notification.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The FGS type launched from BOOT_COMPLETED is on the blocked list for target 35; a different type may be allowed, which is why behaviour varies.
