(b) The user never opened the app since install: stopped-state apps do not receive BOOT_COMPLETED. (c) Direct boot/locked storage: receiver runs before user unlock; BOOT_COMPLETED arrives after unlock, LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED before. (d) OEM autostart blocking.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell am broadcast -a android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED -p com.fit on a debug device; check adb shell dumpsys activity services; read the Android 15 behaviour-changes page for the list; test with the compat flag adb shell am compat enable FGS_BOOT_COMPLETED_RESTRICTIONS com.fit (name: verify with am compat list).
  5. Root cause: Android 15 restricts launching specific types of FGS from BOOT_COMPLETED to reduce boot-time resource use. The design assumed "boot receiver can start any FGS".
  6. Fix: Replace the always-on boot start with:
override fun onReceive(c: Context, i: Intent) {
    if (i.action != Intent.ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED) return
    try { ContextCompat.startForegroundService(c, Intent(c, StepService::class.java)) }
    catch (e: Exception) {            // ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException is API 31+
        NotificationHelper.showResumePrompt(c)       // user taps -> activity -> FGS (allowed: user action)
        WorkManager.getInstance(c).enqueueUniqueWork("resume", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, resumeRequest)
    }
}

Prefer sensor batching (Sensor.TYPE_STEP_COUNTER is cumulative since reboot and hardware-backed, or Health Connect) so no live service is needed to count steps, and reconcile on app open. 7. Prevention: Behaviour-change checklist for every bump; instrumented boot test; telemetry "boot resume outcome". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use exact alarms to start a blocked FGS. Don't ask for SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW as a loophole.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which intent do I listen for with direct boot? → LOCKED_BOOT_COMPLETED with directBootAware; credential-encrypted storage is unavailable until unlock.
  • Is the user notified? → Only if you post it. The system just throws.
  • Does the restriction apply to targetSdk 34? → Per the docs it applies to apps targeting 35; verify.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A tracking app lost a day of step data for 4% of Android 15 users because "resume after reboot" was silently throwing in a receiver, and the exception was swallowed by a try/catch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: battery exemption.
  • Hire: identifies boot FGS restriction and fallback.
  • Strong hire: sensor batching design, direct boot awareness, compat flag testing.

questions.contextHtml:
A checkout flow crashes ~0.3% of sessions (45K sessions/day) with:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.checkStateLoss(FragmentManager.java:1581)
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.enqueueAction
    at androidx.fragment.app.BackStackRecord.commit(BackStackRecord.java:...)
    at com.shop.CheckoutFragment$onViewCreated$2.invokeSuspend(CheckoutFragment.kt:88)

Code:

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    val result = repo.pay(cart)                         // 3-8 s
    parentFragmentManager.beginTransaction()
        .replace(R.id.container, ReceiptFragment())
        .commit()
}

Happens when the user presses Home during payment. The team proposes commitAllowingStateLoss(). Red herring: only occurs on slow networks.
questions.promptHtml: What is the bug and what is the right fix?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use commitAllowingStateLoss." It hides the crash and can lose the navigation step, leaving the user on the payment screen after being charged.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the payment idempotent and persisted? What if the user comes back after process death? Is the result stored somewhere other than the Fragment?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make navigation lifecycle-aware; keep payment result in the ViewModel and a durable store.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) User backgrounded the app, onStop (and on API 28+ onSaveInstanceState after onStop) already ran, state is saved; the coroutine finishes and tries to commit. (b) With lifecycleScope.launch the block is not suspended when below STARTED, so it runs. (c) A second commit raced with Navigation. (d) Reentrancy within onActivityResult.
  4. How I'd verify each: Add a log in the commit path with lifecycle.currentState and parentFragmentManager.isStateSaved; reproduce by pressing Home during a 5 s delay in the repo; check the stack for state; unit test with FragmentScenario moved to CREATED.
  5. Root cause: After state has been saved, the FragmentManager refuses to change the back stack, since the change could not be restored. The code is not tied to lifecycle state.
  6. Fix:
// ViewModel holds result as state
viewModel.payResult.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { /* LiveData only dispatches when STARTED */ }

// or Flow:
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.events.collect { e ->
            if (e is PayDone) parentFragmentManager.commit { replace(R.id.container, ReceiptFragment()) }
        }
    }
}

Use a state-based UI (Pay.Done(receiptId)) rather than one-shot events if the navigation must not be missed; the screen renders the receipt whenever it next becomes visible. Persist the order result so that process death still shows the receipt. 7. Prevention: Lint rule/code review: no FragmentManager commits from coroutines that outlive STARTED; lifecycle tests. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: commitAllowingStateLoss is acceptable only for non-critical UI where a lost transaction is harmless (e.g. a dismissible banner). lifecycleScope.launchWhenStarted is deprecated; avoid.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is state saved after onStop? → On API 28+ onSaveInstanceState is called after onStop; before 28 it was before onStop.
  • Does commitNow help? → No: same check; and it cannot be used with addToBackStack.
  • Does the Navigation component avoid this? → It uses FragmentManager too; navigate() after saved state throws the same error, so the same lifecycle rules apply.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" commitAllowingStateLoss in a payment flow produced support tickets where users were charged but never saw the receipt. The event had been dropped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: allowing state loss.
  • Hire: lifecycle-aware collection.
  • Strong hire: state vs event design, persistence, API 28 callback order, test.

questions.contextHtml:
A cloud-photo-backup app (2M DAU) runs initial library backup (up to 40 GB, 8-14 h on typical connections) in a dataSync foreground service. After targeting 35, support gets complaints that backup stops overnight on Android 15; Crashlytics:

android.app.RemoteServiceException$ForegroundServiceDidNotStopInTimeException: A foreground service of type dataSync did not stop within its timeout: ComponentInfo{com.photos/com.photos.BackupService}

and a milder cluster of backups stopped at ~6 h. The service never implements onTimeout. Red herring: a battery-saver mode report from a few users.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the failure and redesign the long backup.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Restart the service when it stops." Restarting in the background is exactly what is blocked.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the backup user-initiated? Is it resumable at the file/chunk level? Does the user need to see progress? What does Play policy allow us to declare?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Implement onTimeout(startId, fgsType) to checkpoint and stopSelf(); show "Backup paused, tap to continue".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) On Android 15 for apps targeting 35, dataSync (and mediaProcessing) FGS have a budget of about 6 hours in any 24-hour period; the system calls Service.onTimeout, and if you do not stop within a few seconds the app crashes with the exception above (verify numbers on the Android 15 behaviour page). (b) Restart attempts from background hitting start restrictions. (c) Doze interfering at night: contributes but not the crash. (d) Memory kill.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run the service in a test build and use the documented testing approach: adb shell am compat enable FGS_TYPE_DATA_SYNC_DISABLED ... or the timeout test flag (look up with adb shell am compat list, and the Android 15 test docs), or reduce the timeout via a developer flag; log onTimeout events.
  5. Root cause: The service treated FGS as an unbounded run-forever container. Android 15 caps certain types and expects apps to use WorkManager/user-initiated jobs for long transfers.
  6. Fix:
class BackupService : Service() {
    override fun onTimeout(startId: Int, fgsType: Int) {      // API 35
        checkpoint()                                            // persist offsets synchronously, quickly
        stopSelf(startId)                                       // within seconds, or crash
        WorkManager.getInstance(this).enqueueUniqueWork("backup-continue", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, continueReq)
    }
}

Redesign: model backup as WorkManager chunks (constraints: unmetered + charging for the big initial sync); in the foreground, show user-initiated work with a user-initiated data transfer job (API 34+) when appropriate; background continuation runs inside normal job windows. Keep per-file checkpoints so each stop loses at most one chunk. 7. Prevention: Behaviour-change test script; metrics backup_stop_reason (timeout, user, system); alert on the exception. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't try to dodge the timeout by restarting the service immediately (counts against the budget and it is a violation). Don't relabel as another type to bypass the cap; policy declarations (Play Console) catch it. A charging + Wi-Fi gate reduces battery complaints but delays completion.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the timeout reset? → It is a per-24 hour budget, resetting when the app comes to the foreground, per docs; verify.
  • What about mediaPlayback? → No timeout; it has other rules (BOOT_COMPLETED start restrictions).
  • Would an exact alarm every 5 hours help? → It would be a policy and battery violation, not a design.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A backup app discovered its 14-hour "initial sync" had been quietly running for years inside dataSync; the day it was capped, half of the large-library users stalled at 60%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restart loop.
  • Hire: implements onTimeout and moves to WorkManager.
  • Strong hire: budget math, user-initiated jobs, chunked checkpoints, telemetry, policy awareness.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app (1M DAU) targets API 34 and requests READ_MEDIA_IMAGES to show a gallery grid. Since the bump, 7% of Android 14 users report "my gallery shows only 3 photos" or "infinite permission prompt":

val launcher = registerForActivityResult(RequestPermission()) { granted ->
    if (granted) loadGallery() else showDeniedState()
}
launcher.launch(Manifest.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES)

On Android 14, users can choose "Select photos and videos" in the dialog. Result: granted == false, but the app can read some photos. Product claims "denied users see the empty-state". Red herring: the same code works on Android 13.
questions.promptHtml: Explain the behaviour and fix the flow properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Ask again until granted." That violates the UX and the platform's intent.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do we need full gallery access or just a "pick photos" flow? Do we need background re-scans of the library? What is minSdk (13 uses READ_MEDIA_*, <=12 READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Treat partial access as success; read via MediaStore with whatever is visible; offer "Select more".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Android 14 added READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED; if the app only asks for READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, the system still shows the new choice and an app that only checks READ_MEDIA_IMAGES sees "denied" while a partial grant exists. (b) The grant is per-session and may be revoked when the app is closed or the process dies. (c) Permission dialogs after two denials will not re-prompt. (d) MediaStore returning only the selected set is correct.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell dumpsys package com.social | grep -E "READ_MEDIA|granted"; Settings > Permissions > Photos and videos shows "Selected photos only"; test choosing "Select photos" and checking checkSelfPermission for both permissions.
  5. Root cause: Partial access is a third state and the code's boolean model (granted/denied) cannot express it.
  6. Fix:
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_IMAGES"/>
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED"/>
fun accessLevel(c: Context) = when {
    c.has(READ_MEDIA_IMAGES) -> Full
    Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 34 && c.has(READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED) -> Partial
    else -> None
}

Request arrayOf(READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED) together on 34+. On Partial, show the visible items plus a "Manage" button (re-request the permissions to bring up the picker). Better: use the Photo Picker (PickVisualMedia), which needs no permission, unless the product truly needs full library access (Play has a policy limiting broad media access). 7. Prevention: Test matrix: Full, Partial, Denied, "Don't ask again" on API 33 and 34; analytics for permission state. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't nag for full access. Don't copy the whole library to app storage "to be safe". Don't use READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE on 33+; it does nothing for media.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does the photo picker backport? → Yes via Google Play services on API 19+ devices (ActivityResultContracts.PickVisualMedia), verify the availability check isPhotoPickerAvailable.
  • What if the user changes selection in Settings? → The app's process may be killed, similar to any permission change.
  • Why must I declare both permissions? → The new permission has to be in the manifest and requested with the media permission to enable the new dialog behaviour on 34.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An app interpreted partial access as denial and displayed an empty state, and the "infinite prompt" tickets came from users re-selecting photos each session.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: boolean permission model.
  • Hire: handles three states and both manifest permissions.
  • Strong hire: prefers photo picker, covers API-level matrix, and knows the policy constraint.

questions.contextHtml:
A notes app (900K DAU) plans to target API 36. QA on Android 16 reports: the in-editor "Discard changes?" dialog never appears on back swipe, the app exits straight to the launcher, and a bottom sheet closes the whole Activity. The code:

class EditorActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onBackPressed() {                 // deprecated since API 33
        if (viewModel.dirty) showDiscardDialog() else super.onBackPressed()
    }
    override fun onKeyDown(code: Int, e: KeyEvent): Boolean {
        if (code == KeyEvent.KEYCODE_BACK) { handleBack(); return true }
        return super.onKeyDown(code, e)
    }
}

Manifest has android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback="false" from an earlier workaround. Red herring: back button works on 3-button navigation in Android 12.
questions.promptHtml: Why does it break and how do you migrate without regressions on old versions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Keep the opt-out flag." For apps targeting 36 the opt-out is not honoured (verify on the Android 16 behaviour-changes page).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is minSdk? Which screens intercept back (editor, bottom sheet, nested fragment, WebView)? Any libraries overriding onBackPressed? Do we use Navigation (which registers its own callbacks)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hold the targetSdk bump until the editor is migrated; if the deadline is near, ship the callback fix first (works at target 35 too).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) With predictive back system animations enabled, onBackPressed() and KEYCODE_BACK are no longer called for apps targeting 36; back is delivered only to OnBackInvokedCallback/OnBackPressedCallback. (b) The bottom sheet depends on onBackPressed fallthrough. (c) Fragment back stack interplay. (d) Gesture vs button differences.
  4. How I'd verify each: Android 16 emulator with gesture navigation; developer option "Predictive back animations"; adb shell am compat for the predictive-back change id (use am compat list); grep for onBackPressed, KEYCODE_BACK, dispatchKeyEvent.
  5. Root cause: The old model asked the Activity at the moment of press. Predictive back needs to know before the gesture finishes whether the app will handle back, so handling must be registered declaratively with enabled state.
  6. Fix:
class EditorActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val discardCallback = object : OnBackPressedCallback(false) {
        override fun handleOnBackPressed() = showDiscardDialog()
    }
    override fun onCreate(b: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(b)
        onBackPressedDispatcher.addCallback(this, discardCallback)
        lifecycleScope.launch {
            repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
                viewModel.dirty.collect { discardCallback.isEnabled = it }   // enabled only when it matters
            }
        }
    }
}

Remove onBackPressed/KEYCODE_BACK overrides and the opt-out flag; for bottom sheets use the Material component's built-in back progress support or add a callback enabled only while expanded. In Compose, BackHandler(enabled = dirty) or PredictiveBackHandler for progress. 7. Prevention: Lint (OnBackInvokedCallback, deprecated API usage) fails CI; UI tests with pressBack(); screen-by-screen back-behaviour table in review. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not enable callbacks permanently (it swallows system animations, e.g. cross-activity). Avoid onBackPressedDispatcher.onBackPressed() loops. Do not call finish() in a callback that should be disabled.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why enable/disable state matters? → The system decides animation (back to home vs in-app) from whether any enabled callback exists.
  • What about activities with android:enableOnBackInvokedCallback unset on 33-35? → Opt-in per app/activity; verify defaults per release.
  • How do multiple callbacks order? → Last added, enabled callbacks first (LIFO), lifecycle-aware ones only when STARTED.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team had five different back hacks across Activity, Fragment and dialog; the migration found two that silently relied on onBackPressed being called after a dialog dismissed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: opt-out flag.
  • Hire: OnBackPressedCallback with enabled state.
  • Strong hire: full inventory, bottom sheet/Compose handling, tests, awareness of per-version defaults.

questions.contextHtml:
A delivery app (400K DAU) bumps targetSdk 30 -> 31. QA finds on Android 12:

java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: com.delivery: Targeting S+ (version 31 and above) requires that one of FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE be specified when creating a PendingIntent.
    at android.app.PendingIntent.checkFlags

in three places: a notification content intent, a geofence PendingIntent, and an inline-reply notification action (RemoteInput). After adding FLAG_IMMUTABLE everywhere, inline reply still sends empty text and the geofence stops delivering transition extras. Red herring: the crash only occurs at target 31.
questions.promptHtml: Pick the correct flag per case and explain why the "all immutable" patch broke two flows.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use FLAG_MUTABLE everywhere for compatibility." That reopens the hijacking risk the change closed.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who fills in the intent at send time: the system (RemoteInput, geofencing, location updates, bubbles) or only us? Are the intents explicit? What is minSdk (flag exists from API 23)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not in production yet; fix before release.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Immutable PendingIntents cannot have extras/fillIn merged by the sender; the system adds results (reply text, geofence event) to the intent, so those cases need mutability. (b) Implicit base intents with mutable PendingIntents are dangerous. (c) FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT semantics unaffected.
  4. How I'd verify each: Test inline reply and geofence on an Android 12 device; log extras in receivers; lint UnspecifiedImmutableFlag.
  5. Root cause: The platform now requires developers to choose; immutable is right by default, but system components that must write into the intent need FLAG_MUTABLE.
  6. Fix:
// content intent: immutable
PendingIntent.getActivity(ctx, id, intent, PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE)
// inline reply: must be mutable, intent MUST be explicit
val replyIntent = Intent(ctx, ReplyReceiver::class.java).setPackage(ctx.packageName)
val replyPi = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(ctx, id, replyIntent,
    PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT or (if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 31) PendingIntent.FLAG_MUTABLE else 0))
// geofence: mutable on 31+ because Location Services adds the GeofencingEvent

Use PendingIntentCompat.getBroadcast(ctx, id, intent, flags, isMutable) from AndroidX Core to avoid the version branching. 7. Prevention: Lint at error severity; a review rule that every FLAG_MUTABLE is justified in a comment and uses an explicit component. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Never a mutable PendingIntent with an empty/implicit base intent. Don't pass sensitive data in extras; assume any holder can send it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What is the attack? → A malicious holder fills in component/action/data on a mutable PendingIntent with an empty base intent and runs it with your app's identity.
  • FLAG_IMMUTABLE on API 23-30? → Supported from API 23; harmless.
  • Android 14 tightening? → Mutable PendingIntents with implicit intent for apps targeting 34 throw; verify the exact rule.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "make the crash go away" PR set MUTABLE on everything; the security review caught an empty-intent mutable PendingIntent exposed through a notification.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all mutable.
  • Hire: per-case flags with justification.
  • Strong hire: explicit intent requirement, compat helper, security reasoning, lint.

questions.contextHtml: A B2B inventory app (60K DAU, but used in bursts) syncs via a periodic job every 15 minutes and FCM "sync-now" pushes. Support: "after 3-4 days of not opening the app, data is stale for hours and syncs only after we open it." Telemetry: sync success within 15 min is 97% for active users, 31% for users inactive 3+ days. FCM sends use default priority for sync-now. Devices: Samsung/Pixel Android 12-14. Red herring: a recent Retrofit upgrade.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and propose a design that respects battery policy.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the job frequency or use a foreground service." Both worsen standby penalties.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What bucket are stale devices in? Is the sync required in the background or only freshness on open? How much data is fresh-on-open acceptable? Are pushes data-only?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Sync on app open and on resume so the user never waits visibly; keep background sync as an optimisation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) App Standby Buckets: apps unused for days move to Frequent/Rare (and Restricted in some cases); jobs and alarms are deferred more, network access is limited, and FCM normal priority messages are deferred or not woken. (b) Doze deferral overnight. (c) Battery saver/OEM controls. (d) Server not retrying.
  4. How I'd verify each: adb shell am get-standby-bucket com.inv; adb shell am set-standby-bucket com.inv rare; adb shell dumpsys jobscheduler | grep -A5 com.inv; adb shell dumpsys deviceidle; log UsageStatsManager.getAppStandbyBucket() (API 28+) in telemetry; check FCM priority arrival.
  5. Root cause: The design assumed background execution as a right; the platform grants it by how recently and often the user uses the app.
  6. Fix:
// On app open: foreground refresh, always
override fun onStart() { super.onStart(); syncNow(reason = "start") }
// Background: WorkManager periodic with sensible constraints, and no heroic scheduling
PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncWorker>(1, TimeUnit.HOURS)
    .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build())
    .build()

Server: high-priority FCM only for user-visible, time-sensitive events (e.g. a picking task assigned), data-only collapse keys for sync-now; show "last synced at" in the UI. For field devices owned by the company, manage via MDM (exempt from standby) instead of app tricks. 7. Prevention: Test with buckets forced; metric "staleness at open"; alert if background success <80% in Rare bucket is expected and acceptable. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't use REQUEST_IGNORE_BATTERY_OPTIMIZATIONS as the default; Play restricts it. Don't shorten periodic intervals (min is 15 minutes anyway). Don't send everything at high priority.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Do high-priority FCM messages wake a Rare app? → Yes, but with a daily quota (bucket-dependent; verify); beyond it they may be demoted to normal.
  • What does Restricted bucket imply? → Jobs run roughly once per day in a short window, no expedited jobs, alarms restricted.
  • Does exempting from battery optimisation change the bucket? → It exempts from Doze/standby restrictions, but is policy-sensitive.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Support blamed "the sync job". The fix was admitting freshness-on-open was the SLA, then removing a polling loop that had been burning quota and keeping the app in a worse bucket.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increase frequency.
  • Hire: identifies buckets, adds fresh-on-open.
  • Strong hire: priority discipline, MDM path, telemetry on bucket and staleness.

questions.subtopic: End-to-end: notification tap after process death
questions.promptHtml: A user taps a notification two hours after the app was last used. Walk through everything the system and your app do from the tap to the first rendered frame, naming each platform component and each place state can be lost.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It integrates process model, Zygote/AMS, Application init, task stacks, saved state and permissions into one coherent mental model. Seniors can narrate it without hand-waving.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "SystemUI fires the PendingIntent, which asks ActivityTaskManager to start the target activity. If no process exists, AMS asks Zygote to fork one, the process runs ActivityThread, creates the Application (providers first), then the Activity gets created with whatever saved state the system holds. Any state in memory, singletons, or ViewModels is gone, so the screen must rebuild from the intent, saved state and persistent storage."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SystemUI: tap -> PendingIntent.send (runs with OUR identity)
   |
system_server: ActivityTaskManagerService
   |  resolves intent, task placement (launchMode/flags/TaskStackBuilder)
   |  process for app? NO ->
   v
ActivityManagerService -> Zygote (fork, preloaded classes) -> new process
   |
app process: ActivityThread.main -> bindApplication
   |  1. ContentProviders onCreate (incl. App Startup initializers)
   |  2. Application.onCreate
   v
scheduleLaunchActivity: Activity.onCreate(savedInstanceState?)  -> onStart -> onResume
   |  savedInstanceState != null only if the task record has saved state
   |  (not on a fresh task started by the notification)
   v
first frame: ViewRootImpl traversal -> Choreographer -> RenderThread

State inventory:

  • Lost: singleton fields, ViewModels, caches, in-flight network, static flags, in-memory auth token.
  • Kept by system: task record, the saved Bundle (if the old task still exists), intent extras of the PendingIntent.
  • Kept by you: Room, DataStore, files, Keystore keys.
  • Permissions: still granted unless revoked; if revoked the process was killed and relaunch happens without them.
  • Cold start costs: Zygote fork + class loading + provider/Application init, and if baseline profiles are absent, interpretation/JIT.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DetailActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(s: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(s)
        val id = savedInstanceState?.getString("id") ?: intent.getStringExtra("id")
        // Never assume ViewModel has data: load from DB/network by id, show loading state
        viewModel.load(id ?: return finish())
    }
}
adb shell am force-stop com.app && adb shell am start-activity -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d app://x   # measure TotalTime

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming Application state set by a previous screen (e.g. config loaded in Home) exists.
  • Reading only intent or only savedInstanceState; the entry may be either.
  • Doing heavy work in Application.onCreate, which every tap pays for.
  • Forgetting onNewIntent when the task already exists.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does Back go afterwards? → Depends on the PendingIntent: a plain getActivity gives a single-activity task; TaskStackBuilder builds a synthetic stack with parents.
  2. Which components run in which order at cold start? → Providers' onCreate, Application.onCreate, then Activity.onCreate.
  3. How would you prove where the time goes? → am start -W for TotalTime, Perfetto/reportFullyDrawn(), Macrobenchmark StartupMode.COLD (profiling depth belongs to the performance chapter).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "app starts, Activity opens." Senior: names AMS/Zygote/providers/Application ordering, where each category of state lives, and which one is the bug when "it works only if I opened the app first".

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feature opened by notification worked in QA (who always had the app warm) and crashed in the field when a singleton ConfigRepository had not loaded.

questions.subtopic: Post-incident review of a platform-blind release
questions.contextHtml: Release 8.4 (targetSdk 34, 1.8M DAU) went to 100% in 3 days, then a rollback. Timeline: day 1 crash-free users 99.7% -> 98.9% on Android 14; day 2 ANR rate 0.3% -> 1.1% on low-RAM devices; day 3 support spike: "notifications don't open the right chat" and "music stops after locking screen". Changes in the release: targetSdk bump, a new analytics SDK, a refactor moving the token into a singleton, and Media3 migration. Staged rollout was skipped due to a marketing date. QA ran on two Pixel emulators, API 33 and 34.
questions.promptHtml: Run the post-incident review. What went wrong at the platform-awareness level and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Blame the developer for the notification bug and add more tests." No systemic causes, no ordering of fixes, no ownership.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which of the four changes correlates with which symptom (use per-version and per-device cuts)? What alerts fired and when? What was the time to detect and to roll back? Who owned the rollout decision?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt rollout, rollback via Play (halt + hotfix), communicate; keep a feature flag kill switch for the SDK.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Crash on Android 14: missing FGS type/permission or exported-receiver flag (targetSdk 34 behaviours). (b) ANR on low-RAM: SDK initialising on main, binder calls. (c) Wrong chat opened: PendingIntent identity or launch-mode regression. (d) Music stops: FGS or Media3 service change plus OEM kill. (e) Token singleton: process-death crashes.
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics/Play vitals cuts by OS, RAM class, vendor; diff of merged manifests between 8.3 and 8.4; Perfetto on a low-RAM device for cold start; replay with am kill, Doze, locking the screen for 30 min; check dumpsys notification PendingIntents.
  5. Root cause: Process failure, not a single bug: no platform-behaviour checklist for a targetSdk bump, no staged rollout, a narrow device matrix, and four risky changes shipped together.
  6. Fix: Short-term: hotfix the top two causes, re-enable staged rollout. Long-term:
    • Release policy: staged rollout 1/5/20/50/100 with automatic halt gates (crash-free users, ANR rate per device class).
    • Separate targetSdk bumps from feature releases.
    • Behaviour-change checklist (per API level), with compat-flag tests (am compat) in CI.
    • Device matrix: low-RAM, Samsung, Xiaomi, API 29/31/33/34.
    • Platform-resilience test suite (recreate, process death, Doze, permission revoke).
  7. Prevention: Metrics per release in a dashboard; release captain role; blameless review document with action items and owners.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't add a heavy QA gate that delays every release; invest in rollout automation instead. Don't blame an individual. Don't bundle risk to hit a marketing date.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Marketing demands the date; what do you offer? → A 5% staged release plus a server-side feature flag launch on the date.
  • How do you attribute ANRs to a release? → Play vitals by version code and device class; custom keys for SDK versions.
  • Is a rollback possible on Android? → Play can halt; you ship a higher versionCode with the fix; users on bad build remain until update, so a kill-switch via remote config matters.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The review's most valuable action was dull: a release template that forces the author to list platform-facing changes (manifest diff, permissions, targetSdk). It caught the next three risky changes in code review.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames people.
  • Hire: separates causes, proposes staged rollout and device matrix.
  • Strong hire: gates, kill switches, per-cause verification plan, owner-driven actions.

questions.contextHtml: Product says: "Our delivery app must track the courier's location continuously, even when the phone is locked or the app is closed, and it must be battery friendly, and it must not scare users with permission prompts." Fleet: 25K couriers on personal devices, Android 10-14, shifts of 6-8 h. Play review rejected the last submission for background location justification. Prior implementation: a started service plus wakelock; battery drain complaints at 18%/h on mid-range phones.
questions.promptHtml: Turn this into a workable platform design and push back where needed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Request ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION and run a service." That ignores policy, FGS rules and the battery claim.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is tracking only during an active shift/delivery (user-visible)? Required accuracy and frequency (every 5 s vs 30 s)? Do we need data when the app is "closed" or only when a shift is active? Can couriers see a persistent notification?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scope tracking to active delivery windows; lower fix frequency; remove wakelock.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (about the design): (a) A foreground service of type location started from a user action (Start shift) satisfies the platform and policy for continuous tracking while visible via notification; it needs FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION and a foreground location permission (fine/coarse) at start, since Android 14. (b) Background location permission is for tracking without a visible FGS, usually not needed if FGS + ongoing delivery; if used, it is a two-step flow (Android 11+: foreground first, then background through Settings). (c) Fused Location Provider with batching and balanced power is more efficient than raw GPS. (d) Doze affects non-foreground tracking.
  4. How I'd verify each: Battery Historian/Perfetto power rails, adb shell dumpsys batterystats; compare 5 s high accuracy vs 15-30 s PRIORITY_BALANCED_POWER_ACCURACY with distance filter; test shift flow on Android 14 with permission variants; Play pre-launch review of the declaration form.
  5. Root cause: The requirement conflates "visible tracking during a shift" (supported) with "invisible always-on tracking" (restricted by design and policy).
  6. Fix:
val req = LocationRequest.Builder(Priority.PRIORITY_BALANCED_POWER_ACCURACY, 15_000)
    .setMinUpdateDistanceMeters(30f)
    .setMaxUpdateDelayMillis(60_000)          // batching
    .build()
fused.requestLocationUpdates(req, callback, Looper.getMainLooper())
// Service: foregroundServiceType="location", started from a button; ongoing notification "Shift active"

Adaptive rates: stationary -> slower, moving -> faster using Activity Recognition. Stop tracking when the shift ends; keep a visible indicator. Prepare a policy declaration and video showing the prominent disclosure. 7. Prevention: Battery SLO (e.g. <6%/h), tracked in beta; permission-state telemetry. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't hide tracking; policy and trust. Don't accept "continuous high accuracy" without a battery number. Don't request background location "just in case".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the user force-stops mid-shift? → Tracking stops; detect via missing heartbeats server side and notify.
  • Does the FGS survive Doze? → Yes, foreground services keep running, though location updates may still be subject to throttling for background-only access.
  • 5 s granularity needed for safety? → Then raise the notification and battery expectations explicitly and ask the fleet to use chargers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Dropping the update rate from 5 s to 20 s with distance filtering cut drain by more than half, and customers noticed nothing in the ETA accuracy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: background permission + service.
  • Hire: FGS location tied to user action, fused provider tuning.
  • Strong hire: pushes back with numbers, handles policy, permission variants, and failure detection.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through how Android's background-execution rules evolved from Doze to Android 15, and give me a decision rule for choosing between a foreground service, WorkManager, an alarm and FCM today.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Background work questions are the most version-sensitive area. Seniors can place each rule in a timeline and choose tools by the contract each one gives.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Each release tightened what runs without the user: Doze in 6, background service limits in 8, background-start limits and FGS-start restrictions in 12, typed FGS and exact-alarm gating in 13/14, timeouts and boot limits in 15. Today: visible, user-started, ongoing work is a typed foreground service; deferrable, guaranteed work is WorkManager; a time-critical user-facing moment is an alarm or high-priority FCM; and server-triggered work is FCM."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
API 23  Doze (deep), App Standby                      -> idle devices defer jobs/alarms/network
API 24  Doze on the move (light)                      -> screen-off, not stationary
API 26  Background execution limits                   -> bg apps cannot create services; implicit broadcasts cut;
                                                         startForegroundService + startForeground within ~5 s
API 28  Standby buckets                               -> Active/Working/Frequent/Rare (+ Restricted later)
API 31  Background FGS start restricted; exact alarm permission; expedited jobs
API 33  POST_NOTIFICATIONS; USE_EXACT_ALARM; FGS task manager
API 34  FGS types mandatory (+ per-type permissions); SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM off by default for new installs;
        user-initiated data transfer jobs
API 35  dataSync/mediaProcessing timeouts (~6 h per 24 h); BOOT_COMPLETED can't start some FGS types

Decision rule:

Need Tool Why
User-visible, ongoing (music, nav, call, active upload) Foreground service of a proper type System recognises it, notification shows
Must eventually run, can defer, survive reboot WorkManager (JobScheduler under the hood) Constraints, retries, persistence
Must happen at a time the user expects (reminder, alarm clock) AlarmManager exact (with permission) Time-bound; short work then hand off
Triggered by server events FCM (high priority only for user-visible) Efficient wake; subject to quotas
Short work after a user action while app is alive Coroutine in a lifecycle scope No service needed
Key constraints: alarms and FCM only start work; they are not execution environments. Only an FGS or a bounded job window gives you a runtime.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Decision example: user taps "Upload"
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueueUniqueWork("up-$id", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP,
    OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadWorker>()
        .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build())
        .setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)
        .build())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using a foreground service as a persistence mechanism.
  • Scheduling exact alarms for non-time-critical work.
  • Assuming behaviour changes are per OS vs per targetSdk without checking; many Android 12-15 FGS changes depend on targetSdk, whereas Doze and standby apply by OS.
  • Relying on OEM-specific hacks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can WorkManager run immediately? → Expedited work (quota-limited) approximates it; otherwise constraints and system jobs decide timing.
  2. Why 15 minutes minimum for periodic work? → JobScheduler minimum period; flex windows within that.
  3. How do you test across these? → dumpsys deviceidle force-idle, am set-standby-bucket, am compat, and test target and OS versions separately.
